network.overall_strategy: Construct ten condition-specific pathways to alanine, explicitly distinguishing L-alanine from its D coproduct. These include Strecker chemistry, CO2-dependent cyanide chemistry of pyruvate, five mineral/metal-dependent alternatives including oxime reduction, and two thiol-dependent sugar routes. Several pathways are experimentally distinct catalyst variants, not independent reaction mechanisms. Atmospheric discharge supplies Strecker precursors; mineral-mediated CO2 reduction supplies a conditional, dilute pyruvate source. Glyceraldehyde, formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde and hydroxylamine are explicitly external feedstocks where their production is not established here. All synthesis pathways produce racemic alanine. A separate, explicitly conditional circularly polarized light module represents possible modest enrichment, not demonstrated production of enantiopure L-alanine. Its photoproduct representation is marked speculative. The network is complete as a dependency graph, not as a demonstrated integrated geochemical process: concentration, mineral regeneration and terrestrial chiral selection remain gaps. Neutral formulas represent pH-dependent aqueous species; null environment_formed denotes external supply or formation in multiple environments. Mineral electron reservoirs are identified in agents, but their unresolved spent phases are not represented. Roles labeled intermediate also include side products because the schema has no byproduct role.

molecules.common_name: pyruvic acid; predominantly pyruvate under alkaline conditions
pyruvic acid oxime; E/Z configuration unspecified
lactic acid; lactate side-product pool, stereochemistry unspecified

reactions.name: Discharge production and aqueous capture of Strecker precursors

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas-water apparatus; the discharge is nonthermal
conditions.other: Electrical discharge through an anoxic, locally reducing gas mixture with water circulation and aqueous trapping. H2 may also be present initially. The node summarizes selected products of a complex discharge mixture.

reactions.mechanism: Energetic gas-phase fragmentation and recombination generate cyanide and carbonyl compounds, followed by dissolution in water. H2 is included as a possible net dehydrogenation product; this is not an elementary reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1953) and Johnson et al. (2008) support discharge-driven amino-acid precursor production and subsequent Strecker chemistry. The route requires a sufficiently reducing local atmosphere and does not establish a globally methane-rich early atmosphere. Product ratios and precursor concentrations cannot be inferred from this coarse-grained node.

reactions.name: Reversible acetaldehyde-ammonia condensation

conditions.other: Moderately alkaline, ammonia-containing water; approximately pH 8-10 is a proposed environmental window rather than a claimed optimum. The imine is transient and need not accumulate.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, followed by reversible carbinolamine dehydration to ethanimine.
reactions.reasoning: This is established Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850), consistent with Miller's interpretation of discharge-derived alanine (Miller, 1953). Water disfavors imine accumulation, but cyanide trapping can pull the coupled equilibrium forward. Low ammonia activity instead increases competing cyanohydrin chemistry.

reactions.name: Nonenantioselective cyanide capture of ethanimine

conditions.other: Aqueous HCN/CN- and NH3/NH4+ equilibria; no chiral catalyst or chiral irradiation is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the planar imine or iminium carbon from either face, generating equal amounts of the two aminonitrile enantiomers under achiral conditions.
reactions.reasoning: The aminonitrile pathway is supported by classical Strecker synthesis and its prebiotic applications (Strecker, 1850; Miller, 1953). The separate stereoisomer nodes prevent racemic synthesis from being misrepresented as selective L-alanine production.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile hydrolysis to racemic alanine
agents: Acidic aqueous fluid providing proton catalysis

conditions.other: A separate acidic stage, approximately pH 1-3, is proposed after aminonitrile formation. Residence time and natural conversion at these conditions are uncertain. Neutral formulas represent the corresponding protonated species in acidic solution.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration proceeds through an amide and then carboxylic-acid formation, releasing ammonia/ammonium. In the absence of racemization, each aminonitrile retains its alpha-carbon configuration.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis completes established Strecker alanine synthesis (Strecker, 1850; Miller, 1953). Laboratory hydrolysis or analytical workup must not be equated with spontaneous quantitative conversion in a natural pool. Joining alkaline precursor formation to sufficiently effective hydrolysis is an environmental bottleneck.

reactions.name: Mineral-mediated CO2 reduction and C-C assembly to pyruvate
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, as a candidate Fe-Ni catalytic mineral

conditions.pressure: Pressurized H2/CO2 aqueous system; exact experimental pressure is not specified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Alkaline, anoxic water-rock reaction. This node represents a multistep product network, not concerted reduction of three CO2 molecules. Cooling is required before the lower-temperature amination modules.

reactions.mechanism: Mineral-assisted hydrogen activation, carbon-oxide reduction and surface C-C coupling produce a small pyruvate fraction within a broader mixture of reduced carbon compounds.
reactions.reasoning: Preiner et al. (2020) reported pyruvate up to approximately 10 micromolar in an experimental Fe/Ni-mineral CO2-reduction study. That maximum is not assigned here as a guaranteed awaruite-specific yield. The mechanism and concentration bridge to millimolar amination experiments remain unresolved. No pore concentration or thermophoretic enrichment is assumed to have been demonstrated.

reactions.name: CO2-dependent cyanide/ammonia conversion of pyruvate to alanine

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K candidate surface window; stage-specific conditions require verification
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with dissolved inorganic carbon maintained
conditions.other: Cyanide, ammonia/ammonium and CO2/bicarbonate must coexist. This is a coarse-grained reaction sequence including hydrolysis, not an assertion that every intermediate hydrolyzes rapidly at room temperature.

reactions.mechanism: CO2 enables the cyanide/ammonia reaction of the alpha-ketoacid through the hydantoin/N-carbamoyl-type chemistry described in the supplied research summary. Ring processing, hydrolysis and carbon loss are collapsed into the endpoint reaction. NH3 and CO2 occur on both sides to represent exchange and regeneration within the net sequence; no atom mapping is asserted.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the alpha-ketoacid-to-alpha-amino-acid endpoint and the essential role of CO2. The supplied summary does not establish enough intermediate-specific detail to assign a unique hydantoin structure or an exact microscopic sequence here. This route is not modeled as simple cyanide reduction of pyruvate. Cyanide supply, pyruvate supply and hydrolytic processing remain separate constraints.

reactions.name: Fresh FeS-mediated reductive amination of pyruvate
agents: Freshly precipitated FeS: consumable mineral reductant and reactive surface

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm laboratory benchmark; natural interfacial pressure is not established
conditions.other: Approximately pH 9-10, substantial ammonia excess and fresh reactive FeS. Related Fe-based experiments use roughly 0.375-1.5 M ammonia. Protons denote buffered proton equivalents, not an acidic bulk solution.

reactions.mechanism: Carbonyl-ammonia condensation followed by reduction gives alanine. The organic transformation requires two reducing equivalents per alanine; FeS supplies a finite redox inventory and its spent solid composition is not uniquely assigned.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) demonstrated reductive amination using fresh iron minerals. The approximately 50% yield cited in the supplied report comes from a secondary summary and is not treated as a verified alanine-specific value. FeS is not assumed to be a indefinitely regenerating catalyst. High ammonia demand and the dilute upstream pyruvate source limit integration.

reactions.name: Mixed-valence iron hydroxide-mediated reductive amination
agents: Mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) hydroxide material with approximately 1:1 Fe(II):Fe(III)

conditions.other: Approximately pH 10, excess ammonia and incubation up to approximately 72 h. The mixed-valence solid is a finite reactive redox reservoir. Its natural preparation must be anoxic; molecular oxygen is not supplied.

reactions.mechanism: The mixed-valence surface promotes pyruvate-ammonia conversion and electron transfer. An imine-like intermediate is plausible, but the detailed mineral-mediated mechanism is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Barge et al. (2019) reported the strongest alanine outcome near pH 10 and a 1:1 Fe(II):Fe(III) ratio, with approximately 70% alanine and 30% lactate among detected dissolved organics. Pure ferrous and pure ferric end members did not reproduce this result. An anoxic source of the appropriate mixed-valence material is required and is not established by this node.

reactions.name: Reductive amination by electrochemically pre-reduced FeS
agents: Electrochemically pre-reduced FeS containing reactive Fe0 domains; finite reducing reservoir

conditions.other: Reported amination conditions include pH 9.6, 0.5 M ammonia, approximately 5 mM pyruvate and 48 h. Mineral preparation involved approximately -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days; this energy-intensive preparation is not hidden as spontaneous catalysis.

reactions.mechanism: Reduced iron domains deliver electrons to the carbonyl-ammonia reaction system, producing racemic alanine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) observed nearly complete pyruvate conversion under the reported laboratory conditions. Establishing and maintaining an equivalent natural reducing potential is an open geochemical requirement. The millimolar pyruvate and concentrated ammonia benchmark is not directly supplied by rxn_005.

reactions.name: Ni0/H2-catalyzed reductive amination
agents: Accessible Ni0 surface; supported nickel is the laboratory benchmark

conditions.other: Approximately pH 7-8 and 24 h. Screening used approximately 30 mM pyruvate. Lower-ammonia experiments included approximately 6 mM NH3. Natural native-nickel surfaces need not reproduce the activity of engineered supported nickel.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel activates H2 and catalyzes hydrogenation of pyruvate-derived imine species. H2, rather than unaccounted mineral oxidation, supplies the net reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated alanine formation under these conditions and useful conversion at lower ammonia concentrations than most Fe-mineral experiments. Their low-ammonia nickel yield was reported relative to ammonia, not pyruvate. Native Ni availability, passivation, H2 pressure and pyruvate concentration remain limitations.

reactions.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni alloy/H2-mediated reductive amination
agents: Exposed meteoritic Fe-Ni alloy; Aletai meteorite material is the experimental analogue

conditions.other: Near-neutral to mildly alkaline water containing pyruvate and ammonia. The reported meteorite material contained approximately 18 mol% Ni. Metal delivery is distinguished from delivery of preformed alanine.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible nickel-bearing alloy sites activate hydrogen and mediate the same net imine hydrogenation as the supported-Ni route, with different surface composition and competing reactions.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) reported approximately 24% alanine and 43% lactate with Aletai meteorite material. This is a directly tested, geochemically distinct catalyst-source alternative, not a new fundamental reaction mechanism. Weathering and passivation of naturally delivered alloy may substantially reduce activity.

reactions.name: Condensation of pyruvate with hydroxylamine

conditions.other: Hydroxylamine-containing pyruvate solution. The stated environmental window is proposed, not an exact reconstruction of the published amino-acid experiment.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the ketone and loses water to form a pyruvate oxime. E/Z oxime configurations are not resolved in this coarse-grained node.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) support hydroxylamine/Fe0 conversion of ketoacids to amino acids through oxime chemistry. Hydroxylamine is explicitly an external starting material here because a sufficient prebiotic source is not established by the supplied evidence.

reactions.name: Stoichiometric Fe0 reduction of pyruvate oxime
agents: Native Fe0, explicitly represented as a consumed reactant

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous contact with reactive iron metal. Buffering supplies proton equivalents. Surface passivation and competing corrosion can reduce productive electron transfer.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the C=N bond and cleavage of the N-O bond convert the oxime into alanine. The formal transformation requires four electrons per oxime; oxidation of Fe0 to Fe2+ provides the corresponding reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) demonstrated amino-acid production after adding hydroxylamine and Fe0 to their ketoacid chemistry. Unlike two-electron imine reduction, oxime-to-amine conversion requires a four-electron budget. No chiral control is established, and natural hydroxylamine supply remains the principal route-specific gap.

reactions.name: Thiol-enhanced alanine formation from glyceraldehyde and ammonia
agents: 3-Mercaptopropanoic acid as the experimentally tested organic thiol promoter

conditions.temperature: Near ambient; approximately 300 K surface analogue
conditions.other: Long-lived anoxic glyceraldehyde/ammonium solution; reaction times of approximately 60 days. The organic thiol is an externally supplied promoter whose prebiotic production is not included.

reactions.mechanism: A proposed carbonyl-rearrangement pathway involving methylglyoxal-type, hemithioacetal and imine chemistry couples internal oxidation and reduction to amino-acid formation. Unverified individual transient structures are not promoted to molecule nodes.
reactions.reasoning: Weber (1985) observed approximately 0.6% alanine after 60 days with thiol, compared with approximately 0.1% without thiol. This supports the net transformation, not a uniquely established elementary mechanism or selective L production. Low yield, long residence time, side reactions and thiol supply strongly constrain environmental implementation.

reactions.name: Thiol-dependent alanine formation from formose substrates
agents: 3-Mercaptopropanoic acid as the experimentally tested organic thiol promoter

conditions.other: Approximately pH 5.2 and 35 days; formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde and ammonia/ammonium present together. This is the observed mixed-substrate reaction, not an assumed isolated glyceraldehyde synthesis step.

reactions.mechanism: C1-C2 carbonyl chemistry builds reactive C3 intermediates, followed by thiol-assisted rearrangement and nitrogen incorporation. The overall transformation is internally redox-balanced; no external H2 requirement is introduced.
reactions.reasoning: Weber (1998) reported approximately 1.8% alanine on a formaldehyde basis and essentially none without thiol. This is a distinct tested feedstock pathway from rxn_014, although their downstream chemistry may overlap. A separate, selectively producing formose aldol step is not invented because it is unnecessary to represent the experiment.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-mediated pyruvate hydrogenation to lactate
agents: Accessible Ni0 or meteoritic Fe-Ni alloy surface; alternative catalysts, not a required mixture

conditions.other: Conditions overlap rxn_010 and rxn_011. Ammonia activity and surface properties determine competition between ketone reduction and reductive amination.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation of the pyruvate ketone produces lactate without incorporating nitrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly observed lactate alongside alanine, including substantial lactate production with meteorite material. This branch prevents the graph from implying that all reduced pyruvate becomes alanine. Its relative flux is kinetic and cannot be inferred from reaction connectivity.

reactions.name: Competing mixed-valence iron hydroxide reduction to lactate

conditions.other: Competition with rxn_008. Lower pH and strongly ferrous compositions can favor lactate; proton equivalents are supplied by the aqueous buffer.

reactions.mechanism: Mineral-derived reducing equivalents reduce the keto group directly rather than a nitrogen-containing intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Barge et al. (2019) observed pronounced lactate formation at lower pH and with ferrous-rich materials, including conditions that produced no alanine. This experimental result argues against treating arbitrary Fe(II) minerals as interchangeable alanine catalysts.

reactions.name: Competing FeS-mediated pyruvate reduction to lactate
agents: Fresh reactive FeS as a consumable electron donor

conditions.other: A competing branch within the FeS/pyruvate reaction system. Its importance depends on ammonia activity, pH, surface state and mineral aging.

reactions.mechanism: Direct two-electron reduction of the pyruvate carbonyl yields lactate instead of amino-acid formation.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied research identifies lactate as the recurring competing sink in mineral reductive amination, including the Fe-mineral systems discussed by Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003). An FeS-specific quantitative rate or product ratio is not asserted because it is not supplied. This branch represents the chemically supported competition rather than an additional productive pathway.

reactions.name: Conditional L-favoring partial CPL photolysis with a speculative decarboxylation subchannel

conditions.pressure: Ambient pressure is a proposed terrestrial analogue, not a validated experimental equivalence
conditions.other: Partial irradiation of a thin alanine film with circularly polarized UV of a helicity and wavelength that preferentially destroys D-alanine. Both enantiomers are also listed as outputs because some survive. Natural polarized flux, far-UV transmission and a persistent L-favoring sign are unestablished.

reactions.mechanism: Different photodestruction rates can enrich the surviving mixture in one enantiomer; there is no D-to-L conversion. Ethylamine plus CO2 represents an explicitly speculative, atom-balanced photodecarboxylation subchannel, not a verified complete CPL photoproduct inventory. Relative survival and enantiomeric excess cannot be encoded by stoichiometric edges alone.
reactions.reasoning: Meinert et al. (2014) support wavelength- and helicity-dependent asymmetric photolysis of alanine, while Modica et al. (2014) illustrate small irradiation-induced excesses in ice-analogue chemistry. These studies do not establish reliable terrestrial L selection or enantiopure alanine. The particular ethylamine/CO2 product assignment is not established by the supplied research and is a speculative mechanistic surrogate. This module is therefore a candidate modest-enrichment process, not a solved final purification step.

pathways.name: Discharge-fed Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Methane/ammonia/water discharge supplies cyanide and acetaldehyde; imine formation, nonselective cyanide addition and nitrile hydrolysis yield L- and D-alanine. The appended CPL module is conditional and does not establish enantiopurity.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate followed by cyanide/ammonia chemistry
pathways.description: Hydrothermal pyruvate enters the CO2-dependent alpha-ketoacid amination sequence. Cyanide can be supplied by rxn_001. Environmental transfer, concentration and hydrolytic completion are unresolved; the product before conditional CPL processing is racemic.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate with fresh FeS reductive amination
pathways.description: Mineral CO2 reduction is followed by cooling and FeS-mediated amination in ammonia-rich water. Mineral consumption and the micromolar-to-millimolar concentration gap prevent this from being a demonstrated integrated process. Conditional CPL processing follows racemic synthesis.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate with mixed-valence iron hydroxides
pathways.description: Pyruvate is aminated at an alkaline mixed-valence iron interface. Appropriate Fe(II):Fe(III), ammonia availability and competition with lactate are essential. An anoxic origin for the active material is required. CPL enrichment remains conditional.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate with electrochemically activated FeS
pathways.description: Pre-reduced FeS provides a different experimentally tested electron reservoir for pyruvate amination. Establishing the required preactivation potential and concentrated substrates naturally is unresolved. The amination itself is nonenantioselective.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate with Ni0/H2 catalysis
pathways.description: Pyruvate undergoes nickel-catalyzed reductive amination under H2. This route has lower-ammonia experimental support than most Fe-mineral variants, but substrate concentration, native-metal activity and pressure remain conditional. CPL does not provide established homochirality.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate with meteoritic Fe-Ni alloy/H2
pathways.description: Delivered Fe-Ni metal replaces engineered supported nickel as the tested amination surface. This is a distinct catalyst-source pathway, not an independent reaction mechanism. Lactate is a major competing sink, and the synthesized alanine is racemic before conditional CPL treatment.

pathways.name: CO2-derived pyruvate through oxime formation and Fe0 reduction
pathways.description: Externally supplied hydroxylamine traps pyruvate as an oxime, which is reduced by consumed iron metal. Hydroxylamine availability is an explicit upstream gap. The route produces both alanine enantiomers and shares the unresolved enrichment problem.

pathways.name: Glyceraldehyde-ammonia-thiol pathway
pathways.description: A supplied triose reacts slowly with ammonia in the presence of the experimentally tested organic thiol. The net alanine endpoint is demonstrated at low yield, while detailed transient chemistry and thiol provenance remain unresolved. CPL processing is only a conditional extension.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-glycolaldehyde-ammonia-thiol pathway
pathways.description: Supplied C1 and C2 aldehydes produce alanine in the tested thiol-containing mixed-substrate system. This experimentally distinct input route does not assume an isolated glyceraldehyde intermediate. The observed synthesis is low-yield and nonenantioselective; the appended CPL module remains conditional.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The strongest supported route in this submission. Discharge-fed Strecker chemistry is experimentally established by Miller and subsequent studies, and rxn_001-rxn_004 conserve atoms with the supplied coefficient assignments. The imine is appropriately treated as reversible, and hydrolysis produces actual L-alanine alongside D-alanine. However, gas composition, aqueous capture, and hydrolysis conditions are not specified quantitatively. Approval concerns production of L-alanine within a racemate, not demonstrated enrichment. The balanced rxn_019 neither establishes differential D destruction nor validates its proposed ethylamine photoproduct.
suggestions: Specify discharge gas composition, energy input, precursor capture efficiency, and aqueous concentrations; treat rxn_001 as a net inventory rather than a fixed experimental product ratio.
Provide pH, temperature, and residence time for aminonitrile hydrolysis, including compatibility with the preceding aqueous chemistry.
Keep CPL processing optional. Model L- and D-alanine photodestruction separately using wavelength- and helicity-dependent rates, and report both surviving alanine and enantiomeric excess.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied research supports both dilute mineral-mediated pyruvate production and CO2-dependent cyanide/ammonia conversion of ketoacids to amino acids: Preiner et al. (2020) and Pulletikurti et al. (2022), respectively. Accepting rxn_006 as balanceable does not establish its mechanism or actual net NH3/CO2 fluxes. The main network-level weakness is connecting micromolar hydrothermal pyruvate to an appropriately concentrated surface reaction mixture without demonstrated recovery, transport, or concentration. The route produces racemic alanine; conditional CPL processing does not establish selective L production.
suggestions: Assign rxn_005 a specific experimentally tested mineral, temperature, gas pressures, pH, residence time, and measured pyruvate yield.
For rxn_006, publish explicit stoichiometric coefficients and annotate the literature-supported hydantoin/N-carbamoyl chemistry, including cyanide-derived carbon and nitrogen fates.
Quantify pyruvate recovery, cooling, transport, and any concentration step before contact with cyanide, ammonia, and CO2; do not extrapolate concentrated amination yields directly to micromolar feed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Fresh FeS-mediated reductive amination has experimental support from Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003), but the submitted rxn_007 violates conservation. Naming FeS as an agent does not supply its reducing equivalents in the reaction equation. The competing lactate branch rxn_018 is also UNBALANCED. Both omit electron-donor oxidation and its products. Thus this pathway cannot be accepted as chemically closed despite its plausible underlying transformation. The literature additionally requires controlled mineral freshness, alkaline conditions, and substantial ammonia concentrations.
suggestions: Repair rxn_007 using the reduction half-reaction pyruvic acid + NH3 + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> alanine + H2O, doubled for one L and one D product. Couple it to an explicitly balanced oxidation of the actual Fe/S reductant.
Repair rxn_018 using pyruvic acid + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> lactic acid, again coupled to the identified mineral oxidation products. Electrons alone are not a complete network-level source.
Specify FeS preparation and electron capacity, pH near 9-10, experimentally relevant temperature and ammonia activity, and a finite reductant budget or justified resupply mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Barge et al. (2019, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1812098116) support mixed-valence iron hydroxide-mediated alanine formation and competing lactate production. Nevertheless, rxn_008 and rxn_017 are conservation violations in this network: the mineral electron reservoir and its oxidized endpoint are omitted from the stoichiometry. The experimental activity depends strongly on Fe(II):Fe(III), pH, and temperature; a generic mixed-valence mineral label is insufficient to establish those conditions. The reported high alanine fraction also should not be interpreted automatically as isolated yield from all input carbon.
suggestions: Add the actual mineral reactant and spent-phase compositions to rxn_008 and rxn_017. Each alanine or lactate formation requires two reducing equivalents; proton coefficients must also be corrected.
Use explicitly coupled half-reactions: pyruvic acid + NH3 + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> alanine + H2O, and pyruvic acid + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> lactic acid.

Specify mineral Fe(II):Fe(III), ammonia concentration, and reaction conditions. Benchmark against the approximately 1:1 mineral ratio, pH 10, and 70 °C experiment, while preserving the reported yield basis and lactate competition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aav7848) provide strong experimental support for amination using electrochemically pre-reduced FeS containing partially generated Fe0. However, rxn_009 is UNBALANCED: it contains proton equivalents but no represented electron donor or oxidation products. Electrochemical pretreatment is a preparation requirement and finite source of stored reducing power, not evidence of an indefinitely regenerative catalyst. Neither that preparation nor its geochemical implementation is sufficiently specified here.
suggestions: Repair rxn_009 by representing the material's actual oxidizable components and products. If Fe0 is the relevant donor, include its conversion to the appropriate iron endpoint rather than leaving it solely in an agent description.
Account for two electrons per alanine and couple the balanced organic reduction half-reaction to mineral oxidation or a fully specified electrochemical circuit.

Document the pretreatment potential and duration, including the experimental approximately -0.7 V versus SHE preparation, and distinguish this from the subsequent approximately room-temperature, pH 9.6 amination with 0.5 M ammonia.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The organic reduction and hydrogen source are correctly represented in rxn_010, and rxn_016 is a valid competing lactate sink. Kaur et al. (2024) experimentally support Ni/H2 amination under mild temperatures, including useful outcomes at lower ammonia concentrations than many iron-mineral systems. The principal gaps are upstream pyruvate productivity, catalyst identity and availability, maintenance of dissolved H2, and transfer into the cooler amination setting. The label Biochemical does not itself specify a physical environment. L-alanine is produced within the racemate without needing rxn_019.
suggestions: Specify the tested nickel material, support or surface state, loading, and preservation against oxidation or passivation.
Define temperature, pH, ammonia activity, and H2 pressure; distinguish the approximately 22 °C, pH 7-8, 5 bar experiments from untested environmental extrapolations.
Connect the measured pyruvate supply to an alanine/lactate material balance, retaining yield denominators and quantifying cooling, transport, and dilution.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Fe-Ni alloy/H2 reaction is balanceable and supported by Kaur et al. (2024), including experiments using the Aletai meteorite. This is a legitimate experimentally distinct catalyst implementation, not an additional independent mechanism. Its applicability depends on alloy composition, exposed reactive surface, corrosion history, and H2 availability. Substantial lactate production in the cited experiment limits alanine selectivity. As elsewhere, a dilute pyruvate source and conditional CPL module do not establish an integrated enriched-L production process.
suggestions: Define alloy composition, surface preparation or weathering state, loading, and a physically justified supply of accessible metal.
Specify H2 pressure, ammonia concentration, pH, and temperature rather than assuming the broad environment label reproduces the experiment.
Represent alloy-specific lactate competition quantitatively and preserve the distinction between the reported approximately 24% alanine and 43% lactate outcomes.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by Fe0 reduction is chemically coherent and supported by Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019). Unlike the defective mineral-amination equations, rxn_013 explicitly includes Fe0 consumption and Fe2+ production and passes the supplied balance check. Its stoichiometry corresponds to two Fe0 atoms per alanine when iron ends as Fe2+. Declaring hydroxylamine an external feedstock is legitimate; the remaining questions concern supplied concentration, compatibility, and persistence, not a requirement to synthesize every starting material internally. Pyruvate supply and environmental implementation remain conditional.
suggestions: Publish the explicit rxn_013 coefficients and distinguish the four-electron oxime reduction from the two-electron reductive amination pathways.
Specify hydroxylamine concentration, condensation and reduction conditions, Fe0 surface state, competing corrosion, and the fate of dissolved or precipitated iron products.
Quantify transfer of dilute pyruvate into the oxime reaction and retain CPL enrichment as a separate, unvalidated post-processing option.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Weber's glyceraldehyde/ammonium experiments support this balanceable net conversion, including thiol enhancement and low alanine yields over long reaction times. The lumped transformation is not intrinsically invalid merely because its mechanistic intermediates are omitted. However, the network does not identify the thiol agent or specify its loading and environmental availability. External glyceraldehyde is an acceptable stated boundary condition. The approximately 0.6% alanine outcome after 60 days supports formation, not a high-flux route or selective L synthesis.
suggestions: Identify the thiol used and its concentration; distinguish the experimentally used 3-mercaptopropionic acid from untested generic thiol substitutions.
Specify pH, temperature, glyceraldehyde and ammonium concentrations, and residence time, and quantify competing lactate and condensation products.
Annotate the proposed dehydration, hemithioacetal, and imine sequence as a mechanistic interpretation rather than treating rxn_014 as an elementary event.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Weber (1998) supports thiol-dependent alanine formation from formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde, and ammonia. The net equation passes the supplied balance test; no additional external reductant should be demanded solely because this is a sugar-derived route. Nevertheless, the demonstrated approximately 1.8% yield on a formaldehyde basis required prolonged incubation and a particular thiol-containing mixture. The supplied network does not establish those operating conditions or catalyst availability. It produces L-alanine as a component of racemic alanine, while rxn_019 remains conditional.
suggestions: Specify the thiol identity and loading, reagent ratios, and conditions corresponding to the approximately pH 5.2, 40 °C, 35-day experiment.
Preserve the formaldehyde-based yield denominator and account for competing sugar reactions and product losses rather than implying stoichiometric alanine conversion.
Provide reaction-level literature support and a realistic incubation and retention scenario; independently test any proposed CPL enrichment and photoproduct assignment.

evaluation.network_feedback: NOT APPROVED at the network threshold of 0.9. The listed 23 molecule nodes and 19 reaction nodes form a connected graph with consistent identifiers, and several routes genuinely produce L-alanine within a racemic mixture. However, graph connectivity is not chemical closure. The deterministic check identifies five mandatory conservation failures: rxn_007, rxn_008, rxn_009, rxn_017, and rxn_018. These require explicit reducing equivalents, corrected proton stoichiometry, and the corresponding electron-donor oxidation products; agent annotations and acknowledged unresolved spent phases do not repair them. The other 14 reactions are accepted as balanced or balanceable, including rxn_006 and rxn_019, without treating balanceability as proof of mechanism or selectivity. Criterion assessments are network validity 0.70, chemical feasibility 0.63, environmental consistency 0.54, pathway coherence 0.68, target achievement 0.83, and literature alignment 0.78. Experimental support is substantial, and the submission appropriately acknowledges racemic production, dilute pyruvate, external feedstocks, catalyst variants, and integration gaps. Nevertheless, numerical reaction conditions, physical transfer justifications, agent availability, and reaction-level citations are largely absent from the supplied network. Literature conditions cannot simply be presumed implemented. CPL-induced small excesses are supported by the cited Meinert and Modica studies, but this does not establish a terrestrial L-favoring irradiation source, differential photolysis rates, or ethylamine as the relevant product. Enantiopure L-alanine is not demonstrated, although purity was not imposed as a prerequisite for crediting actual L-alanine formation. Pathway membership was inferred from route names and step counts; rxn_019 was treated as optional post-processing, and rxn_016-rxn_018 were scored as side branches where applicable. P1's pathway approval does not imply network approval. Neither the number of catalyst variants, shared molecules, convergence points, nor the number or ordering of environments affected the assessment.
